speaker: Mike Krieger
title: Anthropic's CPO on what comes next | Mike Krieger
question: Among startups building on foundation model APIs, what separates the teams that extract the most value from new model releases?
guest: It is being willing to build at the edge of capabilities—basically breaking the model and then being surprised by the next model. The companies that a new model finally made possible were trying it beforehand, hitting a wall, and realizing the models were almost good enough for power users even if not generally usable yet. We also ran a much broader early access program because we can hill-climb on public evaluations like SWE-bench, Tau-bench, or Terminal-Bench, but customers ultimately know their own real-world benchmark from their own usage and testing. So it is two things: pushing the frontier of the models, and having a repeatable process to evaluate how well your product serves those use cases when you drop a new model in. Some of that is classic A/B testing, some is internal evaluations, some is capturing real traces and rerunning them on a new model, and some is direct hands-on testing. You are not going to feel the leap of a new model unless you are repeatedly throwing a really hard problem at it.

points.core: Top teams build at the capability frontier where current models still break.
points.note: Accept: building workflows that barely work or fail on current models so the next model release immediately unlocks product viability. Do not credit: generic advice to adopt AI early or move fast.

points.core: Public AI benchmarks poorly predict performance on a startup's specific product workflows.
points.note: Accept: standardized leaderboards or academic evals failing to capture real customer usage patterns and domain-specific quality. Do not credit: generic skepticism of benchmarks without contrasting them against product-specific usage.

points.core: Leading teams maintain repeatable custom evaluations using captured production traces across model releases.
points.note: Accept: replaying real user traces, running internal eval suites, or structured A/B testing whenever a new model drops. Do not credit: vague mentions of testing or monitoring without repeatable model-swapping evals.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
The teams that gain most from a new model release are the ones that did the preparatory work before it arrived, and that work is mostly evaluation infrastructure. This is a judgment from widely observed practice, not a measured finding.

They maintain evals built from their own production data and failure cases, so within hours of a release they know whether the new model is better for their specific tasks, where it regresses, and whether it's worth the cost. Teams without these rely on impressions and migrate slowly or blindly.

Second, they keep their architecture thin and swappable. Prompts, scaffolding, and workarounds are treated as disposable, so when a model makes a chain of hacks unnecessary, they delete code rather than defend it.

Third, they build slightly ahead of current capability. They design products that barely work today, so each release turns a marginal feature into a reliable one, instead of optimising around present limitations.

Finally, their durable value lives outside the model: proprietary data, workflow integration, distribution, and domain understanding. A better model then amplifies their advantage rather than commoditising it.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
The startups that capture the most value from new model releases treat upgrades as a repeatable engineering discipline rather than an ad-hoc migration. Their foundational advantage is proprietary, automated evaluation suites built from real production traces and edge-case failures. Instead of relying on public leaderboards or manual spot-checks, these teams know within hours where a new release improves quality, shifts latency and cost, or silently regresses on domain-specific tasks.

Equally important is architectural agility. Top teams decouple core product logic from model-specific quirks and route subtasks dynamically across tiers, applying new frontier models to hard reasoning while shifting newly tractable routine work to faster, cheaper models. When a stronger release arrives, they readily delete brittle prompt workarounds and heavy scaffolding that only existed to compensate for older limitations.

Finally, they design for the trajectory of capabilities rather than static ceilings. Instead of building thin patches around current model weaknesses—value a single API update can erase—they invest in proprietary context, deep workflow integration, and user feedback loops, allowing each model leap to unlock better product experiences immediately.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The teams that gain the most from new model releases usually do four things well.

First, they have good evals. They keep test suites built from real customer tasks and edge cases, so they can score a new model against their own product within hours. Teams without evals depend on vibes and public benchmarks, and they adopt late or poorly.

Second, they build for the models that are coming. They design products that sit just past what current models can do reliably. When a stronger model ships, features that used to be shaky start working, and no rebuild is needed. Teams that tuned everything to today's limits often find new releases make their product obsolete.

Third, they treat scaffolding as temporary. Prompt chains, retries and guardrails added to cover model weaknesses are kept modular and get removed when a model no longer needs them, so complexity doesn't pile up.

Fourth, their advantage lives outside the model. Proprietary data, workflow integration, distribution and feedback loops mean a better base model makes their product better instead of making it a commodity. A model-agnostic setup also lets them switch providers quickly.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
The startups that gain the most from new model releases treat models as rapidly improving, swappable engines rather than fixed constraints. First, they invest early in automated, domain-specific evaluations drawn from real production traffic. When a new model drops, they can benchmark accuracy, latency, and unit economics within hours instead of guessing from demos, allowing them to ship upgrades immediately or route specific tasks to the best-fitting model.

Equally important is architectural restraint. Teams that extract the most value avoid overfitting their products with brittle prompt hacks and rigid, hand-coded scaffolding designed to compensate for yesterday's model limitations. They maintain clean abstractions and routinely delete obsolete workarounds whenever a stronger release can handle more reasoning natively.

Finally, these teams anchor their defensibility outside the model itself—in proprietary workflow data, deep tool integrations, and tight user feedback loops. Because they own the context and the verification layer, every foundation model jump compounds their product's reliability and margins rather than commoditizing it.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
The teams that get the most value from new models already know where the old ones held their product back. They track real customer failures, keep representative tasks ready to rerun, and can quickly test whether a release improves quality, latency, or cost enough to change what they offer.

The biggest gains often come from revisiting a workflow they previously ruled out. A more reliable model might let them automate a step that needed human review. A cheaper one might make a feature viable for every customer. The strongest teams can test those changes with users quickly and measure whether they improve completion rates, reduce rework, or make the product more economical. Their advantage compounds because each release starts with a better understanding of what customers need and where the model still falls short.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
The teams that gain the most know which model limitations are holding their product back and can quickly test whether a release removes them. They keep examples of real customer tasks, especially failures, and evaluate new models on outcomes customers care about: how often a task gets finished, how much human review it needs, what it costs, and how long it takes.

They also revisit product decisions made around the old model’s limits. A modest reliability improvement can create substantial value if it lets a customer review only exceptions instead of checking every result. Teams that own the customer workflow and see where users intervene are best placed to spot those opportunities. Access to the release is widely shared. The advantage comes from knowing which improvement matters and turning it into a better product quickly.
